title: Longitudinal Metabolic Control in Children With Early-Treated Phenylketonuria.
paragraphs: Phenylketonuria is an inherited metabolic disorder caused by phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) deficiency, resulting in elevated phenylalanine concentrations in the blood and brain. 1 , 2 Hyperphenylalaninemia encompasses PAH deficiency and tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency. PAH deficiency is commonly classified by pretreatment peak blood phenylalanine concentration as mild hyperphenylalaninemia (<360 µmol/L; to convert to milligrams per deciliter, divide by 60.544), mild phenylketonuria (360-1200 µmol/L), and classic phenylketonuria (>1200 µmol/L). Treatment is generally recommended when blood phenylalanine concentration exceeds 360 µmol/L. Without timely treatment, persistent hyperphenylalaninemia may cause irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment, intellectual disability, motor dysfunction, and other neurologic and systemic manifestations. 1 , 3 Dietary therapy remains pediatric mainstay, including natural protein restriction, phenylalanine-free tyrosine-supplemented amino acid formula, and low-protein foods. 1 , 4

Newborn screening for phenylketonuria has been implemented in many countries for more than 60 years 5 and in China for more than 40 years, 6 markedly improving prognosis through early detection and intervention. However, long-term metabolic control remains suboptimal 7 and challenging across childhood and adolescence. 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 A 2024 review of dietary adherence in phenylketonuria highlighted the influence of family, patient-specific, environmental, and therapy factors, underscoring the multidimensional nature of long-term management. 16

Previous studies have often focused on specific age periods or used cross-sectional designs, leaving limited longitudinal evidence spanning infancy to late adolescence. 8 , 9 , 14 , 17 Although poor metabolic control has been widely described, less is known about transitions between control states over time and associated factors. To address these gaps, we analyzed longitudinal blood phenylalanine monitoring data from children with phenylketonuria identified by newborn screening and followed up to age 18 years in Beijing, China. Using linear mixed-effects and multistate Cox models, we aimed to characterize age-associated patterns in blood phenylalanine concentrations, first deterioration in annual metabolic control state, and association of demographic, disease-specific, and family socioeconomic factors with long-term metabolic control.

This cohort study was approved by the medical ethics committee of Beijing Obstetrics and Gynecology Hospital (approval No.2025-KY-073-01). Written informed consent was obtained from the legal guardians. This study is reported following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guideline.

This single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted at the Beijing Newborn Screening Center. The source population included patients with hyperphenylalaninemia identified via newborn screening and born in Beijing between 1992 and 2025 who received follow-up at the center. The analytic cohort included early-treated children with phenylketonuria born between January 1998 and February 2024 who had at least 1 year of follow-up and provided informed consent. Blood phenylalanine measurements were collected through March 2025.

Data were extracted from medical records. Follow-up data included serial blood phenylalanine measurements and test dates from outpatient visits or home dried blood spot submission. Blood phenylalanine concentrations were measured using different laboratory methods and converted to micromoles per liter (eMethods 1 in Supplement 1 ). Longitudinal analyses included all available blood phenylalanine measurements from the first posttreatment test result within reference range to before age 18 years. When multiple measurement was available on the same day, their mean was calculated.

Baseline information included demographic characteristics (sex, birth year, household registration, and current residence), perinatal characteristics (gestational age and birth weight), disease characteristics (age at treatment initiation, newborn screening pretreatment peak phenylalanine concentration), and family socioeconomic information (parental occupation, education, and age at the child’s diagnosis). Diagnosis type, categorized as classic phenylketonuria or mild phenylketonuria, was the primary exposure of interest. Family socioeconomic status (SES) and birth year were also examined as key explanatory variables. Additional covariates included sex, household registration, current residence, and parental mean age at diagnosis. Covariates definitions are provided in eMethods 2 in Supplement 1 .

The primary outcome was longitudinal blood phenylalanine concentration. The secondary outcome was the first deterioration in the confirmed annual phenylalanine control state (good to fair and fair to poor). Detailed outcome definitions are provided in eMethods 1 in Supplement 1 .

Baseline characteristics were compared between diagnosis groups using the χ 2 test or Fisher exact test for categorical variables and the t test or Wilcoxon rank sum test for continuous variables, as appropriate. Missing baseline data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations with 20 imputed datasets. Missingness was summarized, and available baseline indicators of disease severity were compared between included and excluded eligible patients.

Age-associated patterns in repeated phenylalanine measurements were examined using linear mixed-effects models, with square root–transformed phenylalanine concentration as the outcome and age modeled with a natural cubic spline. Curves by diagnosis type were estimated from models including a diagnosis × age interaction. Factors associated with the first deterioration in annual confirmed phenylalanine control state from good to fair or from fair to poor were examined using multistate Cox proportional hazards models. Models were fitted sequentially with adjustment for diagnosis type, birth year, family SES, sex, household registration, parental mean age at diagnosis, and current residence. Sensitivity analyses included alternative parameterizations of SES and parental age, complete-case analyses, adjustment for testing frequency, newborn screening phenylalanine concentration, and age at treatment initiation. Time-varying coefficient models were used for variables that violated the proportional hazards assumption. State-occupancy probabilities were derived from the fully adjusted model under a sequential irreversible good-to-fair-to-poor pathway. Additional model, diagnostic, and sensitivity-analysis details are provided in eMethods 3 in Supplement 1 . Analyses were performed from October 2025 to March 2026 using R software version 4.5.1, and 2-sided P values <.05 were considered statistically significant.

Of 380 patients with phenylketonuria identified by newborn screening, 325 met the eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis; 55 were excluded because of loss to follow-up or lack of informed consent (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1 ). Among 325 children with phenylketonuria (179 [55.1%] male; median [IQR] follow-up, 8.32 [5.41-12.26] years) included in the analysis, 227 (69.8%) had classic phenylketonuria and 98 (30.2%) had mild phenylketonuria ( Table 1 ). Baseline disease severity indicators were broadly comparable between included and excluded patients (eTable 1 in Supplement 1 ). Median (IQR) observed phenylalanine follow-up was 8.32 (5.41-12.26) years. Participants contributed 31 188 blood phenylalanine measurements (median [IQR], 88 [1] samples per child; range, 3-326 samples per child).
P values were calculated using available (nonmissing) data (χ 2 test or Fisher exact test for categorical variables; t test or Wilcoxon rank sum test for continuous variables, as appropriate).

Compared with the mild phenylketonuria group, the classic phenylketonuria group had higher newborn screening phenylalanine concentrations (mean [SD], 467.54 [171.66] vs 894.08 [458.71] µmol/L; P < .001) and pretreatment peak phenylalanine concentrations (mean [SD], 742.73 [233.31] vs 2057.48 [573.04] µmol/L; P < .001). Family SES distributions differed between diagnosis groups ( Table 1 ). This difference was attenuated after adjustment for birth year and age at treatment initiation (eTable 2 in Supplement 1 ). Other baseline characteristics were similar between groups.

Metabolic control worsened with age in both phenylalanine concentration and observed annual control state. During the first year of life, the mean (SD) phenylalanine concentration was 197 (76.7) µmol/L, and only 1 patient (0.3%) was in the poor control range. At ages 2 to 3 years, control remained relatively good, with a mean (SD) phenylalanine concentration of 297 (158) µmol/L and 23 patients (7.7%) in the poor control range. Thereafter, mean (SD) phenylalanine concentration and the proportion of children in the poor control range increased with age. By age 6 years, the mean (SD) phenylalanine concentration had increased to 403.8 (188.6) µmol/L, and 42 patients (18.9%) were in the poor control range. Annual phenylalanine testing frequency declined with age and varied within age groups (eTable 3 in Supplement 1 ).

Descriptive annual transitions based on observed control states also indicated limited improvement to better control states (eTable 4 and eFigure 2 in Supplement 1 ). Among intervals beginning in poor control, 63 of 349 intervals (18.1%) improved to fair control and 4 intervals (1.1%) improved to good control, while 174 of 767 intervals beginning in fair control (22.7%) improved to good control.

In the fully adjusted model (model 3), classic phenylketonuria was associated with a 0.82-unit higher square root–transformed phenylalanine level (β = 0.82; 95% CI, 0.16 to 1.47; P = .02) ( Table 2 ). Higher family SES was associated with lower phenylalanine concentrations in a graded manner; compared with low SES, middle SES (β = −1.10; 95% CI, −2.05 to −0.32; P = .007) and high SES (β = −2.00; 95% CI, −2.82 to −1.19; P < .001) were both associated with lower square root–transformed phenylalanine levels. Birth year was not associated with longitudinal square root–transformed phenylalanine concentration (β per 5-year increase = −0.01; 95% CI, −0.29 to 0.28; P = .96).

In the secondary model including diagnosis × age spline interactions, model-estimated phenylalanine concentrations increased with age overall and in both diagnosis groups ( Figure 1 ; eTable 5 in Supplement 1 ). Model-estimated phenylalanine concentrations were similar during infancy but diverged progressively with age, reflecting a greater age-associated increase in classic phenylketonuria than in mild phenylketonuria. The diagnosis × age interaction was statistically significant (eTable 6 in Supplement 1 ).

Solid lines indicate model-estimated phenylalanine concentrations; shading, 95% CIs; dashed lines, phenylalanine concentrations of 240, 360, and 600 µmol/L (to convert to milligrams per deciliter, divide by 60.544). Model-estimated age-specific blood phenylalanine concentration curves were derived from an expanded linear mixed-effects model including a diagnosis-by-age spline interaction. Additional model details are provided in eMethods 3 in Supplement 1 .

Sensitivity analyses were consistent with the main findings. In sensitivity analyses additionally adjusted for annual phenylalanine testing frequency, the main results were unchanged, and more frequent testing was associated with lower square root–transformed phenylalanine levels (β = −0.18; 95% CI, −0.23 to −0.12; P < .001) (eTables 7-9 in Supplement 1 ).

Direct transitions from a good to poor confirmed annual control state were rare (4 events) and were not modeled. A total of 154 first deteriorations from good to fair control state and 70 first deteriorations from fair to poor control state were observed.

In multivariable multistate Cox models ( Table 3 ), for the first deterioration from good to fair control state, classic phenylketonuria was associated with a higher hazard than mild phenylketonuria (hazard ratio [HR], 1.50; 95% CI, 1.08-2.09; P = .02), and high SES was associated with a lower hazard (HR, 0.54; 95% CI, 0.35-0.83; P = .005), whereas more recent birth year was also associated with a lower hazard (HR per 5-year increase, 0.68; 95% CI, 0.61-0.76; P < .001). For the first transition from fair to poor control state, classic phenylketonuria was not clearly associated with hazard compared with mild phenylketonuria (HR, 1.88; 95% CI, 0.84-4.21; P = .12). Compared with low SES, middle SES (HR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.34-1.78; P = .55) and high SES (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 0.59 to 1.94; P = .83) also were not associated with hazard, whereas more recent birth year remained associated with lower hazard (HR per 5-year increase, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.47-0.77; P < .001). Estimated state-occupancy probabilities based on the fully adjusted multistate Cox model showed worsening control with age and poorer control in classic phenylketonuria than mild phenylketonuria ( Figure 2 ; eTable 10 in Supplement 1 ).

Lines indicate estimated probabilities of good, fair, and poor annual control by age; shading, 95% CIs. Estimates were derived from the multistate Cox model under a sequential irreversible first-deterioration pathway (good to fair to poor control).

Proportional hazards tests showed evidence of nonproportionality for birth year in both transitions and for household registration in the fair-to-poor transition (eTable 11 in Supplement 1 ). In time-varying coefficient models fitted to address these departures, the association of more recent birth year with lower transition hazard was stronger at older ages (eTable 12 in Supplement 1 ), whereas estimates for diagnosis and family SES were materially unchanged.

Sensitivity analyses were broadly consistent with the primary models (eTable 13 in Supplement 1 ). Additional adjustment for annual phenylalanine testing frequency did not materially change the main results, and more frequent monitoring was associated with a lower hazard of deterioration from good to fair control state (HR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.91-0.98; P = .002) and from fair to poor control state (HR, 0.92; 95% CI, 0.86-0.99; P = .02).

In this cohort study of 325 children with newborn screening–identified, early-treated phenylketonuria, metabolic control was generally favorable during the first 3 years of life but worsened thereafter. This pattern was consistent across descriptive phenylalanine concentrations, model estimates, and annual control-state probabilities. Classic phenylketonuria was associated with poorer control, whereas higher family SES and more recent birth year were associated with better metabolic outcomes. These findings highlight the challenge of maintaining control beyond early childhood.

The first 3 years of life are particularly important because of rapid brain development and vulnerability to phenylalanine neurotoxic effects. 3 , 18 In our cohort, metabolic control before age 3 years was generally favorable, indicating that early metabolic targets were largely achieved. Adequate early metabolic control is known to reduce the risk of major neurodevelopmental sequelae, suggesting that current screening and treatment systems in our setting are effective during early childhood. 3 , 19 , 20

However, metabolic control worsened with age, consistent with findings from other phenylketonuria cohorts. 3 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 12 , 17 , 21 In our study, blood phenylalanine levels were associated with declining probabilities of good control and increasing probabilities of poor control. Direct transitions from good to poor confirmed annual control state were rare, consistent with a predominantly stepwise deterioration pattern through the intermediate fair control state. Transitions from poorer to better annual control states were infrequent, suggesting that once metabolic control had deteriorated, reestablishing target phenylalanine concentrations was difficult during routine follow-up. This finding is clinically important because suboptimal phenylalanine control beyond early childhood has been associated with adverse neuropsychological outcomes, including impaired sustained attention, visuomotor coordination, and executive functioning. 20 , 22 , 23 In China, dietary therapy remains the cornerstone of phenylketonuria treatment and, for many patients, the only feasible long-term option. 24 Age-related worsening may reflect challenges in maintaining dietary treatment after school entry and during adolescence, when dietary management is less directly supervised and increasingly influenced by social and behavioral factors. 3 , 5 , 9 , 15 , 16 , 25 , 26 Moreover, increasing food intake and gradual transfer of management responsibility from caregivers to patients may further complicate long-term metabolic control.

Diagnosis type emerged as the most important clinical factor associated with long-term metabolic control. Classic phenylketonuria was associated with higher longitudinal phenylalanine levels and a higher hazard of transition from a good to fair control state. Both diagnosis groups showed worsening metabolic control with age, but the deterioration was more pronounced in classic phenylketonuria. This pattern is biologically plausible, given the greater metabolic severity of classic phenylketonuria, including lower residual PAH activity and dietary phenylalanine tolerance. 3 , 27 Our findings support closer monitoring and individualized management for children with classic phenylketonuria. More frequent annual phenylalanine monitoring was associated with a lower hazard of deterioration, although adjustment for monitoring frequency did not materially alter the primary associations.

Higher family SES was associated with better long-term metabolic control. Higher SES was associated with lower phenylalanine levels and a lower hazard of transition from a good to fair control state. This is clinically plausible because phenylketonuria management requires sustained caregiver engagement, dietary knowledge, time, organizational capacity, and financial resources. Families with greater socioeconomic resources may be better able to obtain low-protein foods, maintain regular follow-up, understand dietary guidance, and support long-term adherence. 28 Therefore, SES may reflect not only economic status but also the broader household capacity for chronic disease management. However, the baseline SES difference between classic phenylketonuria and mild phenylketonuria should be interpreted cautiously, as exploratory analyses suggested attenuation after adjustment for birth year and age at treatment initiation.

Birth year showed a different pattern. It was not significantly associated with absolute phenylalanine levels in the linear mixed-effects model, but it was associated with state transitions in the multistate analysis. Children born more recently had a lower hazard of deterioration from good to fair control and from fair to poor control states. This discrepancy may reflect model targets: the linear mixed-effects model captures mean longitudinal phenylalanine level, whereas the multistate model captures maintenance and transition of clinically meaningful control states. More recent birth year likely reflects a cohort association, capturing cumulative improvements in newborn screening, follow-up systems, nutritional product availability, caregiver education, and overall phenylketonuria care organization. 6 , 29 This finding emphasizes the importance of health system development in improving long-term outcomes.

These findings should also be interpreted in relation to treatment targets, which vary across guidelines. European guidelines recommend blood phenylalanine concentrations of 120 to 360 µmol/L up to age 12 years and 120 to 600 µmol/L from ages 12 to 18 years, 1 , 3 whereas the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics recommends maintaining phenylalanine concentrations of 360 µmol/L or less lifelong in individuals with PAH deficiency. 2 , 3 In China, the recommended upper limit after age 12 years has changed from 600 µmol/L 30 to 360 µmol/L. 31 This variability informed our classification of good, fair, and poor metabolic control. Although lower phenylalanine targets may be associated with better neurocognitive and psychosocial outcomes, 1 , 3 , 32 our findings suggest that maintaining phenylalanine concentrations less than 360 µmol/L may be difficult for many patients in routine practice. Diagnosis type and family SES were associated with deterioration from a good to fair control state, but not with progression from a fair to poor control state. Although the estimate for diagnosis type was imprecise, the lack of association for family SES suggests that once metabolic control has worsened beyond 360 µmol/L, achieving and maintaining blood phenylalanine concentrations within the target range may be difficult under routine dietary management alone. These findings support the need for more sustainable long-term management strategies and expanded therapeutic options.

For patients with persistent suboptimal control beyond early childhood, additional approaches may be needed to complement dietary management. Although dietary restriction remains the cornerstone of phenylketonuria treatment, particularly in early life, long-term adherence may be difficult. Approaches such as sapropterin for responsive patients, 3 , 33 enzyme substitution therapy, 3 , 34 and gene therapy 3 warrant further evaluation as potential adjuncts for improving long-term metabolic control, particularly in older children and adolescents who are unable to maintain satisfactory control with dietary treatment alone.

This study has limitations. First, it was conducted at a single center in Beijing, which may limit generalizability. Second, as an observational study based on routine clinical data, residual confounding cannot be excluded. Third, some important factors, including treatment adherence, caregiver support, and changes in management practices over time, were not fully measured. Fourth, missed monitoring may reflect poorer adherence, potentially underrepresenting children with worse metabolic control and introducing selection bias.

In this retrospective cohort study of children with phenylketonuria, metabolic control worsened with age and was poorer in classic phenylketonuria than in mild phenylketonuria. Higher family SES and more recent birth year were associated with better control. These findings support sustained, developmentally informed, risk-stratified management throughout childhood and adolescence and underscore the need for additional long-term management strategies beyond early childhood, including consideration of additional approaches for patients with persistent suboptimal control.

The first 3 years of life are particularly important because of rapid brain development and vulnerability to phenylalanine neurotoxic effects. 3 , 18 In our cohort, metabolic control before age 3 years was generally favorable, indicating that early metabolic targets were largely achieved. Adequate early metabolic control is known to reduce the risk of major neurodevelopmental sequelae, suggesting that current screening and treatment systems in our setting are effective during early childhood. 3 , 19 , 20

However, metabolic control worsened with age, consistent with findings from other phenylketonuria cohorts. 3 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 12 , 17 , 21 In our study, blood phenylalanine levels were associated with declining probabilities of good control and increasing probabilities of poor control. Direct transitions from good to poor confirmed annual control state were rare, consistent with a predominantly stepwise deterioration pattern through the intermediate fair control state. Transitions from poorer to better annual control states were infrequent, suggesting that once metabolic control had deteriorated, reestablishing target phenylalanine concentrations was difficult during routine follow-up. This finding is clinically important because suboptimal phenylalanine control beyond early childhood has been associated with adverse neuropsychological outcomes, including impaired sustained attention, visuomotor coordination, and executive functioning. 20 , 22 , 23 In China, dietary therapy remains the cornerstone of phenylketonuria treatment and, for many patients, the only feasible long-term option. 24 Age-related worsening may reflect challenges in maintaining dietary treatment after school entry and during adolescence, when dietary management is less directly supervised and increasingly influenced by social and behavioral factors. 3 , 5 , 9 , 15 , 16 , 25 , 26 Moreover, increasing food intake and gradual transfer of management responsibility from caregivers to patients may further complicate long-term metabolic control.

Diagnosis type emerged as the most important clinical factor associated with long-term metabolic control. Classic phenylketonuria was associated with higher longitudinal phenylalanine levels and a higher hazard of transition from a good to fair control state. Both diagnosis groups showed worsening metabolic control with age, but the deterioration was more pronounced in classic phenylketonuria. This pattern is biologically plausible, given the greater metabolic severity of classic phenylketonuria, including lower residual PAH activity and dietary phenylalanine tolerance. 3 , 27 Our findings support closer monitoring and individualized management for children with classic phenylketonuria. More frequent annual phenylalanine monitoring was associated with a lower hazard of deterioration, although adjustment for monitoring frequency did not materially alter the primary associations.

Higher family SES was associated with better long-term metabolic control. Higher SES was associated with lower phenylalanine levels and a lower hazard of transition from a good to fair control state. This is clinically plausible because phenylketonuria management requires sustained caregiver engagement, dietary knowledge, time, organizational capacity, and financial resources. Families with greater socioeconomic resources may be better able to obtain low-protein foods, maintain regular follow-up, understand dietary guidance, and support long-term adherence. 28 Therefore, SES may reflect not only economic status but also the broader household capacity for chronic disease management. However, the baseline SES difference between classic phenylketonuria and mild phenylketonuria should be interpreted cautiously, as exploratory analyses suggested attenuation after adjustment for birth year and age at treatment initiation.

Birth year showed a different pattern. It was not significantly associated with absolute phenylalanine levels in the linear mixed-effects model, but it was associated with state transitions in the multistate analysis. Children born more recently had a lower hazard of deterioration from good to fair control and from fair to poor control states. This discrepancy may reflect model targets: the linear mixed-effects model captures mean longitudinal phenylalanine level, whereas the multistate model captures maintenance and transition of clinically meaningful control states. More recent birth year likely reflects a cohort association, capturing cumulative improvements in newborn screening, follow-up systems, nutritional product availability, caregiver education, and overall phenylketonuria care organization. 6 , 29 This finding emphasizes the importance of health system development in improving long-term outcomes.

These findings should also be interpreted in relation to treatment targets, which vary across guidelines. European guidelines recommend blood phenylalanine concentrations of 120 to 360 µmol/L up to age 12 years and 120 to 600 µmol/L from ages 12 to 18 years, 1 , 3 whereas the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics recommends maintaining phenylalanine concentrations of 360 µmol/L or less lifelong in individuals with PAH deficiency. 2 , 3 In China, the recommended upper limit after age 12 years has changed from 600 µmol/L 30 to 360 µmol/L. 31 This variability informed our classification of good, fair, and poor metabolic control. Although lower phenylalanine targets may be associated with better neurocognitive and psychosocial outcomes, 1 , 3 , 32 our findings suggest that maintaining phenylalanine concentrations less than 360 µmol/L may be difficult for many patients in routine practice. Diagnosis type and family SES were associated with deterioration from a good to fair control state, but not with progression from a fair to poor control state. Although the estimate for diagnosis type was imprecise, the lack of association for family SES suggests that once metabolic control has worsened beyond 360 µmol/L, achieving and maintaining blood phenylalanine concentrations within the target range may be difficult under routine dietary management alone. These findings support the need for more sustainable long-term management strategies and expanded therapeutic options.

For patients with persistent suboptimal control beyond early childhood, additional approaches may be needed to complement dietary management. Although dietary restriction remains the cornerstone of phenylketonuria treatment, particularly in early life, long-term adherence may be difficult. Approaches such as sapropterin for responsive patients, 3 , 33 enzyme substitution therapy, 3 , 34 and gene therapy 3 warrant further evaluation as potential adjuncts for improving long-term metabolic control, particularly in older children and adolescents who are unable to maintain satisfactory control with dietary treatment alone.

This study has limitations. First, it was conducted at a single center in Beijing, which may limit generalizability. Second, as an observational study based on routine clinical data, residual confounding cannot be excluded. Third, some important factors, including treatment adherence, caregiver support, and changes in management practices over time, were not fully measured. Fourth, missed monitoring may reflect poorer adherence, potentially underrepresenting children with worse metabolic control and introducing selection bias.

In this retrospective cohort study of children with phenylketonuria, metabolic control worsened with age and was poorer in classic phenylketonuria than in mild phenylketonuria. Higher family SES and more recent birth year were associated with better control. These findings support sustained, developmentally informed, risk-stratified management throughout childhood and adolescence and underscore the need for additional long-term management strategies beyond early childhood, including consideration of additional approaches for patients with persistent suboptimal control.
